post1.text:
Most leaders treat leadership development as a reward for hitting growth targets. That is exactly backwards.

When companies push from $50M toward $500M, the leadership infrastructure has to be built before the revenue demands it. Not after. Companies that wait until the pressure is already on are not building leaders. They are doing damage control.

Here is what scaling companies get wrong:

1. They promote their best operators into leadership roles without asking whether those people are actually wired to lead people through uncertainty. Operational excellence and leadership are not the same skill set.

2. Mid-year is the most revealing leadership moment of any given year. The distance between the leader you committed to being in January and the one you actually are right now tells you everything about your capacity to scale.

3. Leadership gaps at the top do not stay at the top. They cascade down every layer of the organization and show up as retention problems, execution failures, and culture drift.

Your team is watching how you lead right now, not how you planned to lead. What are they seeing?

#Leadership #BusinessGrowth #Scaling

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur asked whether leaders are actually living up to the goals they set for themselves at the start of the year. It is a fair and uncomfortable question.

At Autobahn Consultants, we work with companies scaling from $50M to $500M and beyond, and the pattern we see repeatedly is this: leaders invest heavily in business strategy and almost nothing in their own leadership development. Then they wonder why the strategy stalls.

At scale, you are not just running a business. You are the culture, the ceiling, and the pace-setter for every person beneath you. If your leadership has drifted since January, your business results are already reflecting it.

Do not wait for year-end to course correct. The second half starts now.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMisAFBVV95cUxNTjFYbk5hUVNZeDNsS2prdVh1X2R1NXBpM2dpdUcxcTNKclN2VmNuWTQ2RFhfT3pqVk00bnp5bVl2S1VMUDZhSm5VU1RWLVVqWW95VHVrYmRJYTdSRDB3X1NNZGI5OC1yakR5aXNFX0gtZ2tpbDFJbHhndTMySWUzcWtCSkxnbFJ2UXducXNrZVdMNjQ0TF91a0g1eVVpMmV1aXZPT25kcDRUOGNxbGNyYQ?oc=5

post3.text:
When Buffini and Company recently added three senior executives specifically to support their next phase of growth, they were not just filling seats. They were making a leadership bet on their own future.

That kind of intentional move is exactly what Katherine Slain writes about in Chapter 1 of Rock Your Business, titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It.

Katherine's core argument is not about hiring more leaders. It is about understanding what kind of leader the next stage of your company actually requires, and whether you are willing to become that person before the growth forces the question.

Scaling is not a strategy problem. It is a leadership problem that gets dressed up as one.

The insight that catches most leaders off guard is this: the version of you that built a $50M company may not be the version that can carry it to $500M.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Every growth strategy has a leadership problem hiding inside it. Companies pushing past $50M rarely stall because of bad markets or weak products. They stall because the leaders at the top were built for a smaller company. What got you here is not what gets you there, and most executives find that out far too late to change course without paying a painful price.

post1.text:
Most business owners think about their exit six months before they want out. That is the single most expensive mistake in M&A.

Valuation is not a number you negotiate at the closing table. It is a number you build over years. Entrepreneur recently reinforced this point, noting that companies with documented exit plans years in advance consistently command better terms and attract stronger buyers.

Here is what that means in practice for leaders running $50M to $500M businesses:

First, your EBITDA margin matters less than your EBITDA trajectory. Buyers pay multiples on what they believe comes next, not what you just reported.

Second, customer concentration is a silent valuation killer. If your top three clients represent more than 40% of revenue, sophisticated acquirers will reprice your deal or walk.

Third, management depth is not a soft metric. Buyers are acquiring a business, not a founder. If the company cannot run without you, you are not selling a company.

What would your business be worth today if you had started preparing for exit three years ago?

post2.text:
A recent piece in the U.S. Chamber of Commerce breaks down the core components of building a business exit strategy, and it is worth a read for any founder or CEO in growth mode.

What the article gets right: the fundamentals matter. Clean financials, a clear ownership structure, and a defined timeline are non-negotiable.

What it does not cover is the part that actually moves the needle at the $50M to $500M level. At that scale, exit readiness is not a checklist. It is an ongoing operational discipline. The companies that exit at premium multiples are the ones treating valuation as a management priority years before any deal surfaces.

If you are scaling and have not had a serious conversation about what your business is worth to a buyer today, start there.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMihAFBVV95cUxONERpMjFwUjkzVW8xLTRScUhVWTQ5VUFMS1R5cFY4c2p2eXYzZ3NYc0V0NUlaMmREUXM2N3VSaThYUjhERGNiSmhFTDB5TVBYNEhrOU9WSHRyYThWWUlUY2RYNlVFNkhvVGU4V3h1bXAtVzUwVVh0bG5FOWxmTUNJTTBJYjI?oc=5

post3.text:
Entrepreneur published a sharp reminder recently: the best time to build your exit plan is long before you think you need one. We could not agree more, and it is exactly the territory Chapter 2 of our upcoming book covers in depth.

In "Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond," chapter authors Paul Belair and George Hohman lay out what it actually takes to maximize your multiple before you ever sit across from a buyer.

The chapter is titled "Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit," and one thing it makes clear is that the levers that move your valuation are not financial engineering. They are operational decisions you make two, three, and five years out.

Most owners wait too long. The ones who do not are the ones who walk away with the outcomes they wanted.

Rock Your Business -- available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: The business owners who exit at premium multiples are not the ones who hired the best investment banker. They are the ones who spent years making their company worth buying before any deal was on the table. If you are running a $50M to $500M business, your valuation is being set right now, whether you are paying attention to it or not. Here is what that means and what to do about it.

post1.text:
Most leadership teams don't fail at strategy. They fail at the step between strategy and work that actually gets done.

A recent Forbes analysis confirmed what we see constantly with scaling companies: the gap is not vision, it is accountability infrastructure. Leaders assume alignment because the room nodded during the planning session. That is not alignment. That is politeness.

Here is what separates companies that execute from those that just plan:

1. Strategy must connect to weekly decisions, not annual reviews. If your team cannot trace today's priorities back to the three-year goal, the plan is decoration.

2. The person responsible for execution cannot also be the person who wrote the strategy. Separation of authorship and ownership is not bureaucracy. It is how things get done.

3. Scaling past $50M requires your leadership team to stop treating execution as an operations problem and start treating it as a culture problem.

So here is the real question: when did your leadership team last audit whether daily work is actually moving the strategy forward?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes breaks down exactly why leadership teams stall on strategy execution, and the findings are uncomfortable in the best way.

The core problem is not a lack of smart strategy. It is that most leadership teams at scaling companies build plans for the boardroom and then return to running the business as if the plan does not exist.

At Autobahn, we work with companies moving from $50M toward $500M, and this is one of the most common breaking points we see. The strategy exists. The execution system does not.

If your team has a plan gathering dust, the fix is not a better plan. It is building the operating rhythm that forces the plan into every decision you make.

Read the Forbes piece here and then ask yourself whether your current structure actually supports execution: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiugFBVV95cUxOSXpNczJQdVBKTWlEV0dsby1FaEFGUVg5X1B3Zk9qUGI2bDJMSUxydGhRdURFUUdERXhBRmNzUndTVXhITTREMzMxdk9faE5rUldabk9ld2p2dHdfeXJjVEpMckJ6dFZNckFkTkk5ZmJ5MHRVSm5iSXo2WGlwc0NoeTBvcUYxTF9pbUNmaDB4LUdlNk9pMll0Y01BRTNVYzJObzRrV3pCN19scHYtdThYcHJVUVFYbjFMbkE

post3.text:
The strategy execution problem is not new. But the lesson that cracked it open for us came from an unlikely place: fish food and Nike shoes.

Chapter 3 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled "What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes." Authors Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall bring hard-won experience from operating in industries that look nothing alike on the surface but share the same underlying truth: strategy without a tight execution system is just an expensive guessing game.

One of the insights they share is how the most successful scaling companies stop treating strategic planning as an annual event and start treating it as a daily operating discipline. The mechanics of how they do that might surprise you.

We are not giving the full framework away here. You will need the book for that.

Rock Your Business, the second book from Autobahn Consultants, is available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most companies scaling past $50M have a strategy. Very few have a system that actually executes it. The difference between the two is not more planning sessions or better slide decks. It is an operating discipline that connects every weekly decision to the long-range goal. Here is what that looks like in practice, and why most leadership teams skip it entirely.

post1.text:
Most $50M companies don't have a sales strategy. They have a collection of habits that worked once and never got questioned.

Gartner recently found that AI is saving sales teams significant time but that time savings alone aren't translating into revenue. The reason is simple: you can't automate your way out of a strategic void.

Here's what that means for leaders running scaling businesses:

1. Activity is not strategy. More calls, more tools, more pipeline meetings mean nothing if your team can't articulate why a specific customer should buy from you over anyone else.

2. Revenue growth at this stage requires deliberate segmentation. Who you stop selling to matters as much as who you pursue.

3. Your sales leader needs a mandate, not just a quota. Accountability without authority produces churn, not results.

Companies between $50M and $500M are in the most dangerous growth zone there is. The systems that got you here are actively working against where you need to go.

What does your current sales strategy actually say, and when did you last rewrite it?

post2.text:
A recent piece in abasto.com makes a pointed argument: B2B sales strategies that ignore AI and deep personalization are already falling behind. That is worth taking seriously, especially if your company is in a high-growth phase.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this play out constantly. Scaling companies invest heavily in headcount and tools but skip the foundational work of defining who they sell to, how they win, and what makes their approach repeatable. AI and personalization are multipliers. They amplify a strong strategy and expose a weak one.

If you are leading a company past $50M in revenue, now is the time to audit your sales foundation before layering in more technology.

Read the full article and then ask yourself whether your current approach would survive that audit.

post3.text:
The conversation around AI and B2B sales is loud right now. But underneath all of it is a problem that technology cannot fix on its own: most growing companies never built a real sales strategy in the first place.

Chapter 4 of Rock Your Business, titled Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation, was written by Deb and Brandon for exactly this reason. The chapter name is not a metaphor. Every day your team operates without a clear, documented sales strategy, you are handing revenue to competitors who have one.

One of the core insights in the chapter challenges leaders to separate sales motion from sales strategy. They are not the same thing, and confusing them is one of the most expensive mistakes a scaling company can make.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling someone gets when they walk into your office, open your packaging, or read your invoice.

Most $50M+ companies treat marketing like a campaign machine. They launch, measure, pause, repeat. JBL recently flipped this model entirely, shifting their marketing focus from campaigns to culture. The result is a brand that people feel before they can explain why they trust it.

Here is what growth-stage leaders need to understand:

First, brand is an operational asset, not a communications asset. It lives in how your team answers the phone, not just how your agency writes copy.

Second, consistency at scale is harder than creativity at launch. Companies scaling past $100M often fragment their brand without realizing it.

Third, your customers can smell inauthenticity faster than any focus group can measure it.

If your brand is being managed only by your marketing department, it is already out of control.

What does your brand actually feel like to someone who has never heard your pitch?

#Branding #BusinessGrowth #MarketingStrategy

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive spotlights how Ulta's CMO is threading together brand building and omnichannel marketing into a single, unified strategy rather than treating them as competing priorities.

This is exactly the tension we see in companies scaling from $50M toward $500M. Leaders often separate brand and performance marketing into different silos with different budgets, different teams, and different definitions of success. That split is expensive.

When brand and channel strategy are disconnected, you end up with inconsistent customer experiences and wasted spend. The companies that grow efficiently are the ones that treat every channel as a brand touchpoint, not just a conversion mechanism.

If your CMO and your channel leads are not in the same room making decisions together, that is worth fixing now.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPRlFnSEozTXJJdnl5aWFJQTFGR0tkcnhrUnUyOTNZNlIwcHZiLWFnbm0tQ0FWZEZCTWZvdUFQeEFvQkIwOHdpMmZBR3I5WmNjRmFYb0xJMGhQWmJHYUdWUVdyWndOWTYwR1ZQQ2E4V1dMV2NrT0hpRzNaU1VKdUdoZHMwSFB4SlhYTkZKZ2hDdEdsSkJ6TW91UTZTWlNGaGVmcUE

post3.text:
JBL is making headlines for building marketing around culture rather than campaigns. It sounds like a creative choice. It is actually a structural one.

Chapter 5 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled "What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?" Authors Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West dig into exactly this challenge for scaling companies. Brand identity does not drift because leaders stop caring. It drifts because growth outpaces the systems designed to protect it.

One of the sharpest insights in this chapter is that by the time most executives notice a brand problem, the internal culture has already been telling customers the same story for months.

If your marketing feels different than it did when you were half your current size, there is a reason for that. This chapter helps you find it and fix it.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

As headcount climbs and new channels multiply, the original identity that made customers trust you starts to blur at the edges. By the time leadership notices, customers already have. Here is what scaling companies need to understand about keeping their brand sharp when everything else is moving fast.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost strategy disguised as ambition.

Companies scaling from $50M toward $500M almost always hit the same wall: they built headcount when they should have built capability. SHRM's latest research confirms it. The firms winning in 2026 are making fewer, more deliberate hires and getting dramatically more from each one.

Here is what that means in practice for leaders at your stage:

1. Your next hire should solve a specific constraint, not a general workload problem. If you cannot name the bottleneck, you are not ready to hire for it.

2. Onboarding is not HR's job. It is a revenue event. How fast someone reaches full contribution directly affects your growth trajectory.

3. The talent decisions you make between $50M and $100M set the culture ceiling for everything above it. Bad fits compound faster than good ones.

Growth does not come from a bigger team. It comes from the right team, moving in the same direction.

What is the one role at your company where precision would matter more than speed right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM lays out what the research is showing about hiring in 2026: volume is out, precision is in. Companies that chased headcount growth are now quietly recalibrating, focusing on fewer hires who fit tighter, better-defined roles.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this is not a trend to watch. It is a decision to make right now.

At Autobahn, we see it constantly. Scaling firms that invest in defining roles with precision before posting them close faster, retain longer, and waste far less leadership time cleaning up mismatched expectations.

Precision hiring is not slower. It is just smarter. And at your stage, smart compounds.

Read the full SHRM piece and then ask your team: do we hire with precision or with urgency?

post3.text:
Companies that scale successfully do not just hire well. They build what our new book calls a Talent Engine.

Chapter 6 of Rock Your Business, written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West, tackles exactly what it takes to turn your people function into a true driver of growth, not just a support function.

With companies like Ouster and WorkWave recently appointing Chief People Officers to lead their next stage of expansion, the signal is clear: talent leadership is moving to the front of the growth conversation.

One thing Chapter 6 makes plain is that most scaling companies already have the talent they need to grow. What they lack is the structure to unlock it. That distinction changes everything about how you lead and hire.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

Precision hiring, intentional onboarding, and treating people decisions as revenue decisions are separating the firms that scale cleanly from the ones that stall. post1.text:
More KPIs do not make your business smarter. They make it slower.

Most companies scaling past $50M fall into the same trap: they keep adding metrics because tracking more feels like managing more. It is not. It is noise dressed up as discipline.

Oracle NetSuite recently broke down the KPIs that actually matter in a complex, fast-moving industry like hospitality. The takeaway applies well beyond that sector: the companies performing best are not tracking the most numbers. They are tracking the right ones with ruthless consistency.

Here is what leaders at your stage need to hear:

1. A KPI without an owner is just a number on a dashboard nobody acts on.
2. When every department has 15 metrics, nothing is actually a priority.
3. The real test of a good KPI is whether a bad result triggers a decision, not a meeting.

You built a $50M business by paying attention. Scaling to $500M means knowing what to stop watching.

What is one metric your team tracks that nobody has acted on in the last 90 days?

post2.text:
A recent piece in business.com rounded up 14 tools designed to help businesses track KPIs more effectively. Solid list, useful for teams just getting started.

But here is what that article cannot tell you: the tool is never the problem.

Companies scaling from $50M to $500M do not fail at KPIs because they picked the wrong software. They fail because they never agreed on which numbers actually reflect business health versus which numbers just look good in a board deck.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. Leadership teams invest in better dashboards while the underlying metrics are still disconnected from strategy. Faster access to the wrong data is not progress.

If you are evaluating KPI tools right now, start with a harder question: do your current metrics drive decisions, or do they just document what already happened?

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that every leadership team at a growing company needs to read before their next planning session.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business is titled "Death by KPIs." Co-authored by Héctor Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, it confronts something most executives quietly know but rarely say out loud: your metrics may be working against your growth.

The chapter does not argue against measurement. It argues against the accumulation of measurement without accountability. There is a meaningful difference between a company that tracks performance and one that is actually managed by it.

One thing the authors make clear is that the number of KPIs in your business is not a sign of sophistication. In many cases, it is a sign of avoided decisions.

If your dashboards are full but your direction feels foggy, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most companies are using AI to save time. The ones that win will use it to make better decisions.

There is a difference, and it is costing mid-market leaders more than they realize.

Harvard Business Review recently surfaced something scaling companies need to hear: the metrics we use to evaluate performance were built for a pre-AI world. When AI handles execution, the old scorecards stop telling you what actually matters.

Here is what that means for leaders running $50M to $500M businesses:

1. Output volume is no longer a proxy for employee value. AI inflates it. Start measuring judgment, not throughput.

2. Your highest performers may look average on legacy KPIs. Recalibrate before you misread your talent.

3. Decisions happen faster now. If your review cycles still run quarterly, you are managing in slow motion.

AI does not just change how work gets done. It changes what leadership actually is.

Are your performance systems measuring the right things for the company you are building today?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Bloomberg gathered AI productivity strategies from 12 CEOs and executives, and one pattern stood out: the leaders getting the most from AI are not using it as a search engine. They are using it as a thinking partner built into their daily operating rhythm.

For companies scaling past $50M, this distinction matters. At that stage, the bottleneck is rarely effort. It is decision quality and leadership bandwidth. AI deployed inside a smart operating system compounds both.

The CEOs in that Bloomberg piece are not ahead because they found a better tool. They are ahead because they changed how they work, not just what they work with.

If you are leading a growing company and AI still feels like an add-on, it is time to rethink the integration.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMirwFBVV95cUxNc010ZUhURC0wVGNKMTdRUWVyTnZFVXRWODBxaVc3MWYyeU52bG1PdHVaTU45aS1mSG13Ulh2eUtmcU5qNXhma2VDLWo0UlpDLWMyU0lZc1ZkcHZzZXVrVXlpNGNObGVxRnVTMlVBc2RQLTk2bWtJaWFmeW1BMlBHNml5SktYdEdaLWJ3VmpYTU55bHB6cVpUVW5LWG1WR2lhRng0SXYwcHdFYXJTanJn?oc=5

post3.text:
Harvard Business Review is now making the case that AI demands an entirely new approach to performance management. Chapter 8 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, has been living in that exact territory.

The chapter is called The Third Monitor Theory, written by Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain. The title alone raises a question most leadership teams have not asked themselves: what is the role AI should be playing at the center of your operations, not at the edge?

The insight that shapes the whole chapter is this: AI is not a department, a tool, or an initiative. For companies scaling toward $500M, it has to become part of how the leadership system itself runs.

The companies figuring this out now are building an advantage that will be very hard to close later.

post1.text:
The most dangerous leader in a scaling company is not the one who doubts themselves. It is the one who stopped doubting themselves too soon.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a problem to fix. At the $50M to $500M growth stage, it is actually a signal worth reading carefully.

Forbes recently reported that high achievers carry self-doubt all the way to the top, and the ones who navigate it best are not the ones who eliminated it. They are the ones who learned to work alongside it.

Here is what that means for leaders scaling a business:

First, persistent self-doubt in capable leaders often reflects accurate pattern recognition, not weakness. You are seeing real risk others are missing.

Second, the leaders who perform best under scaling pressure tend to separate the feeling of being unqualified from the fact of being unqualified. Those are rarely the same thing.

Third, if your leadership team never voices uncertainty, that is not confidence. That is a culture problem.

So the real question is this: are you building a company where doubt gets processed, or one where it just gets hidden?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fast Company argues we should stop calling it imposter syndrome altogether. The label, they suggest, misframes a normal human response to high-stakes growth as a personal defect.

That reframe matters enormously for companies scaling past $50 million.

When leaders at that stage pathologize their own self-doubt, they often overcorrect. They perform certainty they do not have, stop asking hard questions, and build teams that mirror their false confidence back at them.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern consistently. The terminology leaders use to describe their internal experience shapes how they lead. Call it a syndrome and you try to cure it. Understand it as useful data and you start using it.

Read the full Fast Company piece and then ask yourself how your organization actually treats uncertainty at the top.

post3.text:
The most common question we hear from leaders running $50M to $200M companies is some version of this: how did I get here, and does anyone actually believe I belong here?

Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business, titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?", goes directly at that question. Authors Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo wrote this chapter because imposter syndrome does not shrink as companies grow. In many cases, it scales right alongside revenue.

What the chapter reveals is that the feeling of not belonging at the top is not random. There is a specific leadership profile it targets, and understanding that profile changes how you respond to it.

The insight is not about eliminating doubt. It is about knowing when your doubt is working for you and when it is working against your company.

post1.text:
The most dangerous moment in a scaling business is not a cash flow crisis. It is the moment the founder forgets they are a person, not just a CEO.

Morgan Stanley recently published research on what happens to entrepreneurs after they sell. The emotional and identity disorientation many experience is not a post-exit problem. It starts forming years earlier, quietly, while revenue grows and personal life shrinks.

Here is what leaders scaling past $50M rarely hear:

1. Your calendar is a life plan in disguise. What it contains right now is a direct statement about your values, whether you chose those values or not.

2. Burnout at the $100M stage is not about workload. It is about losing the thread of why you started.

3. Designing your personal life with the same rigor you apply to your P&L is not a luxury. It is a retention strategy for yourself.

The business can survive a bad quarter. Can it survive you running on empty for three years straight?

What would you find if you audited your life the same way you audit your operations?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune, produced in partnership with Morgan Stanley, maps out the emotional and financial journey entrepreneurs face after selling their businesses. It is a thoughtful read, but here is what it does not say loudly enough: most founders wait until the exit to think about what comes next. That is too late.

At Autobahn, we work with companies scaling from $50M to $500M and beyond. The leaders who struggle most after a liquidity event are the ones who never built a life independent of the company while they were building the company.

Life planning is not retirement planning. It is an active leadership discipline that pays off long before any transaction.

Read the full article and then ask yourself: what am I building toward, beyond the number?

post3.text:
Fortune and Morgan Stanley just reminded the business world that selling a company without a life plan in place can unravel even the most successful founder. We have been thinking about this for a long time.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, was written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain for exactly this reason. It addresses something most business books skip entirely: the human being running the company.

One of the chapter's core ideas is that life planning and business planning are not separate exercises. When leaders treat them as disconnected, they tend to optimize one at the direct expense of the other, and the business always wins in the short term while the person pays the price later.

There is a framework inside this chapter that changes how scaling leaders think about their time, energy, and identity. We will leave it there for now.
